title: Address Poisoning: The Lookalike Address in Your History
summary: Address poisoning is a scam that targets copy-and-paste habits. An attacker creates a wallet address whose first and last few characters match one you have recently transacted with, then sends you a tiny or zero-value transfer from it so the lookalike shows up in your history.
blocks: Address poisoning is a scam that targets copy-and-paste habits. An attacker creates a wallet address whose first and last few characters match one you have recently transacted with, then sends you a tiny or zero-value transfer from it so the lookalike shows up in your history.

The trap springs later. When you go to pay a familiar recipient, you copy what looks like their address from your recent transactions — but it is the attacker's lookalike, and a transfer on a blockchain generally cannot be reversed.

Most wallets and explorers shorten addresses to their opening and closing characters, which is exactly the part the attacker has matched. Unexpected dust or zero-value transfers from an unknown address are a common sign your wallet has been targeted.

Safer habits: save trusted recipients in your wallet's address book and send from there, check the full address rather than just its ends, and use a small test transfer before sending a larger amount to a new recipient. Never copy a destination from your transaction history.
